records.quote:
By and by I got to musing
over the hour's strange adventure, and of course my human curiosity
began to work. I set myself to framing in my mind some questions for
this fiend to answer.
records.paraphrase: The narrator deliberately formulates questions to investigate the nature of the visible Conscience.

records.quote: Well, I am your Conscience!
records.paraphrase: The strange being reveals itself to be the narrator's Conscience personified.

records.quote:
I killed thirty-eight persons during the first two weeks--all of them
on account of ancient grudges. I burned a dwelling that interrupted my
view. I swindled a widow and some orphans out of their last cow
records.paraphrase: Freed from his Conscience, the narrator commits many crimes without remorse.

records.quote:
You behold before you a man whose life-conflict is
done, whose soul is at peace; a man whose heart is dead to sorrow, dead
to suffering, dead to remorse; a man WITHOUT A CONSCIENCE!
records.paraphrase: The narrator declares his transformed state as a man now entirely without a conscience.

records.quote:
The more I weakened, the more stubbornly you
fastened on to those particular sins; till at last the places on my
person that represent those vices became as callous as shark-skin.
records.paraphrase: The Conscience describes a mechanism by which repeated sinning makes it shrivel and grow callous.

records.quote:
No. It only made me visible to you. I am unsubstantial, just as other
spirits are.
records.paraphrase: The Conscience explains it is an unsubstantial spirit made visible only to the narrator.

records.quote:
The management had provided a microscope
with a magnifying power of only thirty thousand diameters, and so nobody
got to see him, after all.
records.paraphrase: A publisher's conscience is described as so tiny it required a powerful microscope to view.

records.quote:
With a long-drawn sigh my conquered Conscience closed his eyes
and fell fast asleep!
records.paraphrase: Under the aunt's pleading, the Conscience is overwhelmed and falls asleep, defenseless.

records.quote:
Straightway the door opened, and a shriveled, shabby dwarf entered. He
was not more than two feet high.
records.paraphrase: A tiny deformed being suddenly enters the narrator's room.

records.quote:
I tore him to shreds and fragments. I rent the
fragments to bits. I cast the bleeding rubbish into the fire
records.paraphrase: The narrator destroys and burns his Conscience.

records.quote: For a very good reason. I am invisible to all but you.
records.paraphrase: The Conscience states the rule that only its owner can perceive it.

records.quote:
In an instant I was in a blaze of joy and exultation. I sprang at the
creature, roaring:
records.paraphrase: The narrator reacts to learning the being's identity with joyful rage and an attempt to attack it.

records.quote:
Whenever a person whose conscience I am acquainted
with tries to plead with you about the vices you are callous to, I get
my friend to give his client a pang concerning some villainy of his
own, and that shuts off his meddling
records.paraphrase: The Conscience explains a cooperative system among consciences to divert would-be moral pleaders.

records.quote:
When you
were eight or nine years old, I was seven feet high, and as pretty as a
picture.
records.paraphrase: The Conscience explains its size changes over a person's life according to their conscientiousness.

records.quote:
That man walked the
floor in torture for forty-eight hours, without eating or sleeping, and
then blew his brains out. The child was perfectly well again in three
weeks.
records.paraphrase: A disproportion is drawn between a man's conscience-driven suicide and the trivial harm that provoked it.

candidate.quote:
Otherwise it must have occurred to you that if you attempted this
murder with a sad heart and a heavy conscience, I would droop under the
burdening in influence instantly.
candidate.paraphrase: The Conscience explains that its weight and position depend on the narrator's emotional state.

criteria.rationale: The story is a moral allegory/fantasy about a personified Conscience. References like the microscope's magnifying power or 'scientific purposes' are comic exaggerations and satirical decoration, not material representation of scientific facts, theories, or speculative sciences.
No engineered device, technique, or invention materially affects the setting or outcome. The microscope is a passing comic prop; the plot turns on a supernatural Conscience, not technology.
The story is set in the narrator's ordinary contemporary world. There is no speculative future, remote past, or temporal displacement; recollections of the past are ordinary memory, not time travel.

The tale develops consequences from a fantastical premise (a Conscience made tangible and killable): systematic exploration of how it shrinks, sleeps, and cooperates, culminating in the narrator's guilt-free crime spree. This is extrapolation from an imaginative premise, but the premise is supernatural/satirical rather than an identifiable scientific or technological one, so materiality is uncertain.

The narrator merely frames curious questions to his Conscience; this is ordinary interrogation, not observation, hypothesis testing, measurement, or evidential revision materially driving understanding or action. Mere question-asking does not constitute scientific method.

The Conscience is an unsubstantial spirit visible only to its owner, arriving from outside ordinary reality. This resembles a nonordinary visitor, but it is a supernatural/allegorical personification rather than an extraterrestrial, dimensional, or cosmic entity, so materiality to the criterion is uncertain.

The killing of the Conscience and the ensuing personal crimes are individual acts of violence, not a natural, technological, cosmic, biological, or human-caused large-scale disaster. No catastrophe on the required scale is actual, impending, remembered, or causally central.

candidates.description: The narrator's Conscience is externalized as a physical, embodied being (a shriveled dwarf) that operates according to a systematic, immanent set of rules: it is a spirit visible only to its owner, its size and condition reflect the owner's moral history, it grows callous through repeated sinning, it can sleep when a vice becomes callous, and it can be physically seized and destroyed. Conscience-beings form a whole social order (a Conscience Club, cooperative networks, exhibitions). The core world-altering difference is that conscience is a separable, killable entity whose destruction leaves a person able to sin freely without remorse.

novelty.rationale: The reification of an abstract moral faculty into a separate, embodied, destructible creature is a totalizing difference from the empirical norm. Its destruction changes the narrator's whole moral universe, culminating in remorseless mass crime, a world-altering consequence for the protagonist and those around him.

cognitive_validation.rationale: The story develops a coherent, systematic, immanent pseudo-scientific/social logic: consciences are unsubstantial spirits visible only to their owner (a stated rule), their stature tracks the owner's moral development over a lifetime, repeated sin produces callousing like shark-skin, and consciences form an organized cooperative institution with mutual aid. This is imaginary social/psychological science rather than supernatural appeal; the narrator even subjects it to inquiry. Twain frames Satan as explicitly rejected, keeping the account nonsupernatural and rule-governed.

narrative_hegemony.rationale: The embodied, killable conscience determines the entire narrative logic: the whole story is the confrontation with it, the dialogue explaining its nature, the aunt's pleading that lulls it to sleep, its destruction, and the resulting carnival of crime. Every plot beat derives from the premise; it is not an incidental device.

estrangement.rationale: Reader estrangement arises from the grotesque contrast between an abstract faculty and its shabby physical embodiment, the disproportion of conscience-torture versus trivial harm, and the exhibition of consciences too small to see under a powerful microscope, all defamiliarizing the everyday notion of conscience.

candidates.description: The management's microscope with a magnifying power of thirty thousand diameters used to try to display a publisher's minuscule conscience at an exhibition.

novelty.rationale: The microscope is an ordinary-in-kind instrument invoked for comic hyperbole about a tiny conscience. It introduces no totalizing or world-altering difference of its own; it is a derivative joke depending entirely on the conscience novum.

cognitive_validation.rationale: The instrument is only a satirical prop; there is insufficient evidence to assess any systematic account beyond the comic conceit of an invisibly small conscience.

narrative_hegemony.rationale: The microscope appears in a single incidental aside and does not govern the narrative logic; it is an ornamental gadget, not a determining device.

estrangement.rationale: The image of needing a thirty-thousand-diameter microscope to glimpse a man's conscience produces a comic reader-facing contrast, but this estrangement is parasitic on the conscience premise rather than independent.
